title: What sets the safe buckling load of an imperfect cylindrical shell?
summary: Can manufacturing tolerances and loading uncertainties be converted into a mechanics-based lower envelope for cylindrical-shell buckling, and what nonlinear instability realizes that worst case?

statement.lead: Let P_cl be the classical perfect-cylinder buckling load and let 𝒜 be a physically admissible class of geometric imperfections and loading/boundary variations. Define
equations: P_{\rm safe}=\inf_{w_0\in\mathcal A}P_{\rm cr}(w_0),\qquad \kappa_{\rm safe}=P_{\rm safe}/P_{\rm cl}.
statement.after: The open target is to derive a useful lower envelope from the declared admissible class, identify the sharp or near-sharp imperfection family, and connect the minimizing geometry to the nonlinear localized/global buckling mechanism.

why: Thin cylindrical shells achieve exceptional load capacity at low mass but are among the most imperfection-sensitive structures in mechanics.
Engineering design therefore uses knockdown factors and conservative lower envelopes; the fundamental question is how a manufacturing tolerance should be converted into a guaranteed stability margin.
A mechanics-based result could separate truly dangerous defect spectra from harmless imperfections and explain when localized single-dimple states control collapse.
scope: Primary setting: thin circular cylindrical shells under axial compression, with shell theory, end conditions, loading protocol, imperfection metric, amplitude and admissible wavelength spectrum stated explicitly.
The core problem is robust stability over a physically justified imperfection class, not the buckling load of one prescribed dent.
Composite anisotropy, pressure, combined loading, residual stress and manufacturing statistics are extensions that must be declared rather than hidden inside one universal factor.

boundary.text: Modern design practice, including NASA SP-8007 Rev. 2, already uses updated empirical/analysis-based knockdown guidance. The open problem is not the absence of usable engineering design rules.
Mountain-pass theory identified localized single-dimple states as organizing structures in the nonlinear energy landscape of axially compressed cylinders.

Nonlinear continuation later linked localized states to a lower-bound buckling load that correlates with a large body of experiments, strengthening the mechanics connection between energy barriers and knockdown.

Recent 2026 work shows that small changes in defect geometry can switch the triggering bifurcation and produce nonmonotone/discontinuous thresholds and mode changes, reinforcing that the admissible imperfection class cannot be summarized by one amplitude alone.
Additional recent stochastic/engineering lower-bound work addresses uncertainty in imperfection-sensitive shells but does not replace the need for a sharp physically grounded worst-case class.

No general result was identified that converts a realistic declared imperfection/tolerance class into a validated lower envelope with a proved or certified near-worst-case nonlinear mechanism across relevant shell slenderness and boundary conditions.

settle: Freeze the shell model, boundary/loading protocol, admissible imperfection class and norm. Then bound the critical load uniformly over that class and identify the sharp or near-sharp imperfection family.
Connect the lower-envelope geometry to the bifurcation/energy-barrier mechanism and state when the controlling instability is localized versus global.
Validate the resulting lower envelope against independent experiments or high-fidelity computations without fitting away the assumptions that define the class.

progress.title: Defect geometry shown to switch the triggering bifurcation
progress.text: Recent continuation calculations demonstrate that small changes in imperfection geometry can reorganize the localized stability landscape and change the collapse threshold non-monotonically.

progress.title: Modern NASA shell-buckling guidance consolidated
progress.text: SP-8007 Rev. 2 incorporates modern knockdown approaches and the Shell Buckling Knockdown Factor program into current design guidance.

progress.title: Localized single-dimple route linked to lower-bound design load
progress.text: Continuation and experimental comparison strengthened the connection between localized mountain-pass states and engineering knockdown factors.
